narrative:
The model estimates a 25% chance that you will fail your final year, which is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses to strengthen your preparation.

The prediction is driven mainly by three key aspects of your situation. The strongest factor is that you have already failed one class in the past. Among students who passed, the average number of prior failures is zero, so this history pulls the prediction noticeably toward failing. The second most important influence is your reason for choosing this school: you selected it because it is close to home. This choice is less common among students who ultimately pass and works against a passing outcome. The third factor is that you do want to pursue higher education. This intention is actually helpful and pushes the prediction back toward passing, but unfortunately it is not strong enough to outweigh the other two influences.

To improve your chances, focus first on preventing any further setbacks in your current subjects. Because past failure had the biggest impact, creating a realistic study schedule that exceeds the two hours per week you currently spend could help break that pattern. Consider talking with your teachers about targeted support in the areas where you struggled before. Small, consistent changes in study habits and attendance are likely to have the greatest effect on moving your outlook from “at risk” to “on track.”
